## The opening and the board (10)

<p class="rev-plan">Say these from memory before every mock. The two layouts are the minute budgets you write in the corner of the board. Remember the board as a route: corners, spine, centre, bottom, mouth.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="opening-script" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">SCRIPT</span><span class="rev-q">The 3-minute opening script?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

1. Restate in one sentence: "So we are building X for Y users, and the hard part is Z." (10 s)
2. Three clarifying questions, picked from: scale today and in two years · the one latency that matters · read or write heavy · what must never be lost · what is out of scope. Write the answers in the requirements corner as you get them. (90 s)
3. Name the load-bearing categories aloud and cross out the rest: "This is Compute and Bandwidth; storage and memory are ordinary here." (15 s)
4. Say the plan: "I will do requirements and numbers in ten minutes, the design in fifteen, then two deep dives, and I will leave five minutes for failures. Stop me whenever you want to go deeper." (15 s)
5. Then start writing; never start drawing before the numbers are on the board.

**Remember by.** restate, three questions, cross out categories, say the plan, then write; numbers before any drawing.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="opening-script">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="sentences" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">SCRIPT</span><span class="rev-q">The five sentences that carry the interview?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- "Because X is a requirement, I need Y."
- "The alternatives I see are A and B. I prefer A because … The cost of that choice is …"
- "At 10× this breaks at Z first; here is how I would notice, and here is the mitigation."
- "This is a hotspot because …; I would partition by … and accept … as a consequence."
- "The failure I worry about most is …; recovery works like …; the blast radius is …"
- "Let me trace one write end to end to check the design holds."
- "At 10× this breaks first at …; I'd notice via …; mitigation is …"
- "I'm not sure about …; I'd validate by …"

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="sentences">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="layout-scale" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">LAYOUT</span><span class="rev-q">Board layout when scale drives the design: the eight blocks with minute budgets?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

1. 0-8 min: Requirements, top-left
2. 8-13 min: Numbers, top-right
3. 13-17 min: API, left
4. 17-21 min: Data, left under API
5. 21-36 min: Diagram, center, in draw order
6. 36-52 min: Two deep dives, annotate the boxes
7. 52-57 min: Failures and trade-offs, bottom
8. 57-60 min: Summary, said not written.

**Remember by.** a route on the board: corners first (requirements top-left, numbers top-right), the spine down the left (API, then data), the centre (diagram, then the deep dives written onto its boxes), the bottom (failures and trade-offs), and the mouth (the summary is spoken, never written).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="layout-scale">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="layout-diagram-first" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">LAYOUT</span><span class="rev-q">Board layout for a functional-heavy prompt, diagram first?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

1. 0-5 min: The agent loop (only if the first prompt is "Build a coding agent", otherwise these minutes go to requirements)
2. 5-10 min: Requirements, top-left (accept what is dictated, compress, move)
3. 10-24 min: Diagram, center, in draw order
4. 24-26 min: One line of numbers, top-right
5. 26-32 min: API and data, left
6. 32-48 min: Two deep dives, annotate the boxes
7. 48-55 min: Failures and trade-offs, bottom
8. 55-60 min: Summary, said not written.

**Remember by.** the same route with the centre moved up: corners, centre, one numbers line, spine, deep dives on the boxes, bottom, mouth.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="layout-diagram-first">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="functional-rule" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">LAYOUT</span><span class="rev-q">The prompt is functional-heavy and the interviewer wants the diagram first. The rule?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

This prompt is functional-heavy. The interviewer dictates the requirements, asks for the agent loop and the architecture, and does not want a GPU bill: model infrastructure is out of scope and cost is declared infinite. Numbers cover only what you buy: sandboxes, model calls, storage. On a functional-heavy prompt, say the one numbers line before drawing if nobody objects. If the interviewer asks for the diagram first, draw and put the numbers line right after the diagram. The board below uses the diagram-first order.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="functional-rule">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="flow-50" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">FLOW</span><span class="rev-q">The 50-minute flow: phases, minutes, and what each is scored on?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

| Minutes | Phase | What the interviewer is scoring |
|---|---|---|
| 0-5 | Requirements: functional, non-functional, scale, **dominant constraint** | Do you ask the right questions and pick what matters? |
| 5-10 | Estimation: QPS, bandwidth, storage/day and /year, connections, workers, cache size, partitions | Are your numbers in the right order of magnitude, and do you use them later? |
| 10-15 | API and data model, only what matters | Can you define contracts crisply? |
| 15-30 | High-level architecture + trace one flow end to end | Does every box earn its place? Can you follow a request through it? |
| 30-42 | Deep dive on one or two areas the constraint points to | Depth where it matters; tradeoffs stated with costs |
| 42-48 | Attack the design: hotspots, partitioning, replication, consistency, failure, retry, recovery, backpressure, caching, observability, capacity, tail latency | Do you find your own weaknesses before the interviewer does? |
| 48-50 | Summary: what you built, what you would do next, what you are unsure about | Judgment |

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="flow-50">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="principal" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">FLOW</span><span class="rev-q">What a Principal-level interviewer expects to see?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- You drive. The interviewer should rarely need to steer.
- Numbers first, technology names second. "Because we need 40 GB/s of reads across 100 PB, I need N nodes at X GB/s each" beats "I'd use S3."
- Name the alternative you rejected and what it would have cost.
- Operability is part of the design: how you deploy, observe, degrade, recover.
- Say what you do not know and how you would find out.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="principal">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-communicatio-structure-the-hour" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Communication: structure the hour?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Say the plan first: "I'll do requirements, numbers, API, architecture, then go deep on X and attack the design." Then keep to it and announce transitions.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-communicatio-structure-the-hour">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-communicatio-habits" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Communication: habits?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- Numbers before names. Draw only boxes that earn their place; label arrows with what flows.
- Check in briefly every 10 minutes: "Should I go deeper here or move on?"
- When corrected, integrate it out loud instead of defending.
- Time-box: if a deep dive passes 12 minutes, summarise and move.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-communicatio-habits">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-communicatio-coding-rounds-same-principle" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Communication: coding rounds (same principle)?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Restate → clarify → naive → waste → optimal → invariant → code while narrating → test edge cases → time → space. Silence longer than ~30 seconds should be broken with "I'm considering … versus …".

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-communicatio-coding-rounds-same-principle">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Requirements and the phrases that signal the pattern (19)

<p class="rev-plan">What you write in the first eight minutes, and the words in a prompt that tell you which pattern is coming.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-requirements-functional-requirements-2-minutes" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Requirements & non-functional requirements: functional requirements (2 minutes)?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- List the 3-5 things the system must do. Cut everything else explicitly: "Out of scope: X, Y."
- Identify the primary actors and the one flow that matters most (the "money path").
- Ask: read-heavy or write-heavy? Who are the clients (humans, services, GPUs)?

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-requirements-functional-requirements-2-minutes">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-requirements-non-functional-requirements-2-minutes" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Requirements & non-functional requirements: non-functional requirements (2 minutes)?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

| Dimension | Ask | Typical answer shapes |
|---|---|---|
| Availability | How many nines? What is the cost of a minute down? | 99.9 % (8.7 h/yr) · 99.99 % (52 min/yr) |
| Latency | p50 vs **p99** targets per operation | 10 ms cache · 100 ms API · seconds for jobs |
| Consistency | Read-your-writes? Monotonic? Linearizable? | Strong for money/metadata, eventual for feeds |
| Durability | Can we lose data? How much? | 11 nines for storage; at-least-once for events |
| Scale | Users, QPS, data volume, growth per year | Drive the estimation page |
| Cost | Is there a budget ceiling? | Changes tiering, replication factor, regions |
| Security / tenancy | Multi-tenant? Isolation? | Affects quotas, auth, noisy-neighbour control |

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-requirements-non-functional-requirements-2-minutes">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-requirements-the-dominant-constraint-1-minute-the-most-import" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Requirements & non-functional requirements: the dominant constraint (1 minute, the most important sentence)?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Say it out loud: *"The thing that shapes this design is ___."* Examples: 100 PB capacity at low $/GB; 3 MB random reads at very high aggregate throughput; GPU idle cost; exactly-once payment; sub-100 ms fan-out to millions. Every later decision refers back to it.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-requirements-the-dominant-constraint-1-minute-the-most-import">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-requirements-questions-i-always-ask" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Requirements & non-functional requirements: questions I always ask?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- What is the read:write ratio? What is the hottest key/object?
- What happens if this is unavailable for 10 minutes? For a day?
- Is there a natural partition key? Is there a natural time dimension?
- What must never happen (double charge, data loss, duplicate GPU job)?

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-requirements-questions-i-always-ask">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Numbers (20)

<p class="rev-plan">Facts and shapes of calculation. Say the value or the formula, then open.</p>

<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">NUMBER</span><span class="rev-q">One server?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

~10⁴-10⁵ simple requests/s; ~10⁴ concurrent connections comfortably

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="num-one-server">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="num-compression" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">NUMBER</span><span class="rev-q">Compression?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

text 3-10×, video already compressed (~1×)

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="num-compression">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="shape-qps" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">SHAPE OF CALCULATION</span><span class="rev-q">How do you compute QPS?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

QPS = daily ops / 10⁵; peak = 2-5× average.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="shape-qps">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="shape-bandwidth" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">SHAPE OF CALCULATION</span><span class="rev-q">How do you compute Bandwidth?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Bandwidth = QPS × payload size (bytes/s → ×8 for bits).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="shape-bandwidth">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="shape-storage-day" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">SHAPE OF CALCULATION</span><span class="rev-q">How do you compute Storage/day?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Storage/day = writes/day × object size × replication (or × 1.5 for erasure coding); **/year** × 365; add index/metadata ~1-5 %.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="shape-storage-day">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="shape-connections" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">SHAPE OF CALCULATION</span><span class="rev-q">How do you compute Connections?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Connections = concurrent users × connections each; long-lived (chat, streaming) ≠ request/response.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="shape-connections">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="shape-workers" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">SHAPE OF CALCULATION</span><span class="rev-q">How do you compute Workers?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Workers = arrival rate × service time (Little's law: L = λW); add headroom 30-50 %.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="shape-workers">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="shape-cache-size" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">SHAPE OF CALCULATION</span><span class="rev-q">How do you compute Cache size?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Cache size = hot fraction (often 20 %) × working set; hit rate you need = 1 − (backend capacity / total load).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="shape-cache-size">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="shape-partition-size" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">SHAPE OF CALCULATION</span><span class="rev-q">How do you compute Partition size?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Partition size = total / target-per-shard (e.g. 50-100 GB per hot shard, 1-2 TB per cold shard).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="shape-partition-size">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="six-lines" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">SIX LINES</span><span class="rev-q">The six lines in the room, in four minutes?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

In the room: 4 minutes, six lines (1 objects and users; 2 the constraining rate, operations per second or bytes per second; 3 ingress against egress, and growth; 4 the hot set; 5 capacity against IOPS; 6 network ports). The rest is ammunition for probes.

**Remember by.** six words in order: count, rate, in and grow, hot, check, wire.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="six-lines">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="five-categories" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">CATEGORIES</span><span class="rev-q">The five estimation categories: the question each answers, its unit, and when it is load-bearing?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

| Category | The question | Six-line method line | Typical unit | When it is load-bearing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Traffic | How many operations per second, average and peak, and which operation is the constraint? | Line 2, the constraining op/s (from line 1, objects and users) | QPS, writes/s, messages/s, frames/s | Chat, feeds, gateways, rate limiters, search, payments: anything where a request is the unit of work |
| Bandwidth | How many bytes per second in and out, and what is the ratio? | Line 3, egress against ingress; line 6, network ports | MB/s, GB/s, Gbps; ports of 10 or 100 GbE | Video, media, object storage, backups, checkpoints, log pipelines: anything that moves large blobs |
| Storage | How many bytes total, per day, per year, and on how many devices? | Line 3 growth; line 5, capacity against IOPS | TB, PB, disks | Blob stores, data lakes, archives, event logs kept for audit |
| Memory | What must sit in RAM or SSD to meet latency, and does it fit on one box? | Line 4, the hot set | GB, TB, nodes | Caches, timelines, session maps, indexes, order books, ANN vectors, tries |
| Compute | How many GPUs or cores, when the work per request is heavy? | Line 2 again, when the unit is a frame, a token or a match, divided by throughput per device | GPUs, cores, tokens/s, frames/s | Model serving, transcoding, embedding, training, matching engines |

**Remember by.** the life of a byte: it arrives (traffic), moves (bandwidth), lands (storage), stays hot (memory), gets worked on (compute). A causal chain, not an acronym.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="five-categories">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="step-zero" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">CATEGORIES</span><span class="rev-q">Step 0, said aloud before any number?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

"Before I size anything: this is a Traffic and Memory system, storage and bandwidth are small here, and there is no heavy compute. So I will size the request rate, the hot set, and check that the hot set fits in RAM on a handful of nodes." Then the six lines. Then the sentence that names the one number that forced the design.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="step-zero">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## API shapes (17)

<p class="rev-plan">Six shapes as six nouns: one answer, open pipe, ticket, bytes first, page, guard. For each, the request, the response and what gets probed.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="api-sync-request-response" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">API SHAPE</span><span class="rev-q">API shape: Sync request/response. When, the request and response, and what gets probed?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**When.** one input, one answer, seconds

**Request and response.** `POST /v1/<verb> {inputs, options}` + bearer auth + `Idempotency-Key` → `200 {id, result, usage, version}`; `429 + Retry-After`; `4xx` validation

**What the interviewer probes (say these unasked).** retry: same key returns the stored answer, no second charge (24 h record) · timeout: client retries with backoff, server keeps working · long answers: stream tokens (SSE), first token in under a second, `max_tokens` cap · version: alias by default, pinned version allowed, `Deprecation` header for 90 days · large inputs by `file_id`, not inline · `request_id` in a response header for disputes

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="api-sync-request-response">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="api-streaming-session" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">API SHAPE</span><span class="rev-q">API shape: Streaming session. When, the request and response, and what gets probed?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**When.** live data in, results out, state between messages

**Request and response.** `POST /v1/sessions {client_id, model, options}` → `{session_id, gateway_url, token, expires_at, version}`; up `{session_id, seq, ts, payload}`; down `{result_seq, ts, type, payload, version}` + control messages

**What the interviewer probes (say these unasked).** **resume**: `POST /sessions/{id}/resume {token, last_result_seq}` inside a grace window (60 s), server resends only results after last_result_seq, nothing replayed, nothing lost · acks: client acks result_seq, server keeps unacked results for the grace window · heartbeat every few seconds, 3 misses = dead · token expires and is renewed over the open socket · control messages down (granted rate, backpressure) · version pinned for the session's life, never switched mid-stream · explicit close releases quota at once · byte-rate cap per session

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="api-streaming-session">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="api-async-job" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">API SHAPE</span><span class="rev-q">API shape: Async job. When, the request and response, and what gets probed?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**When.** minutes to hours of work

**Request and response.** `POST /v1/jobs {file_ids, options, callback_url}` + `Idempotency-Key` → `202 {job_id, state}`; `GET /jobs/{id}` → `{state, progress}`; `GET /jobs/{id}/results?cursor`; `DELETE /jobs/{id}`

**What the interviewer probes (say these unasked).** same key + same body → same job, same key + other body → 409 · state machine with named states · progress in chunks, partial results pageable as chunks finish · chunk retries with backoff, dead-letter after N, the job reports the failed chunk · webhook signed and retried for 24 h, idempotent on the receiver · results expire (TTL) · priority: jobs run at the lowest weight on spare capacity

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="api-async-job">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="api-upload" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">API SHAPE</span><span class="rev-q">API shape: Upload. When, the request and response, and what gets probed?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**When.** bytes larger than a request

**Request and response.** `POST /v1/files` → presigned URL + `file_id` (expires in minutes); multipart `PUT ?upload_id&part=N` idempotent per part; `complete {parts, checksums}` → READY

**What the interviewer probes (say these unasked).** bytes never cross the API servers · checksum per part and at complete · abort cleans incomplete uploads (lifecycle rule) · size and format validated before READY · the file_id is referenced by later calls, never the bytes

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="api-upload">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="api-read-list" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">API SHAPE</span><span class="rev-q">API shape: Read / list. When, the request and response, and what gets probed?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**When.** feeds, search, dashboards

**Request and response.** `GET /v1/<thing>?cursor=&limit=` filters in the query, tenant from the token never the body → `{items, next_cursor, as_of}`

**What the interviewer probes (say these unasked).** keyset cursor, not offset, so inserts do not shift pages · limit capped · `as_of` or watermark says how stale · ETag / If-None-Match for caching · "seconds stale is fine" said aloud when it is

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="api-read-list">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="api-write-with-a-guard" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">API SHAPE</span><span class="rev-q">API shape: Write with a guard. When, the request and response, and what gets probed?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**When.** booking, inventory, money

**Request and response.** `POST ... {resource, amount, version}` + `Idempotency-Key` → `201` or `409` conflict, `402` payment required

**What the interviewer probes (say these unasked).** optimistic version (If-Match) or a conditional update on the row · holds with TTL and a limited number of extensions · saga with compensation across shards, no 2PC · the retry after a timeout must find the existing record, not create a second

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="api-write-with-a-guard">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="api-fields" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">API SHAPE</span><span class="rev-q">Which fields always exist in the API?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Fields that always exist: `id`, `created_at`, `version`, `request_id` header, `usage` or `cost` where billing exists, `Retry-After` on every 429 and 503.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="api-fields">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="apid-sync-vs-async" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI API DESIGN</span><span class="rev-q">API design for AI and infrastructure services: sync vs async?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- **Sync** (request → result in one call): only when the work reliably finishes within the client's timeout (say < 10-30 s). Simple, but ties up connections and fails badly under load.
- **Async / job API**: `POST /jobs` → `202 {job_id}`; `GET /jobs/{id}` → status; results via `GET /jobs/{id}/result`, webhook/callback, or a message. Use when work is long, variable, or scarce-resource-bound (GPUs). Always for video processing.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="apid-sync-vs-async">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="apid-job-api-essentials" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI API DESIGN</span><span class="rev-q">API design for AI and infrastructure services: job API essentials?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

States: `queued → running → succeeded | failed | cancelled` (+ `retrying`). Fields: id, tenant, created/started/finished, attempts, priority, model version, input refs, output refs, error code. Support cancel, list with filters + cursor, and TTL for results.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="apid-job-api-essentials">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="apid-idempotency" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI API DESIGN</span><span class="rev-q">API design for AI and infrastructure services: idempotency?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Clients retry; the network duplicates. Every create/mutate accepts an `Idempotency-Key`; the server stores key → response for a window and returns the same response on replay. Downstream operations are made idempotent by natural keys (e.g. `(job_id, attempt)`), upserts, or compare-and-set on versions.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="apid-idempotency">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="apid-retry-semantics" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI API DESIGN</span><span class="rev-q">API design for AI and infrastructure services: retry semantics?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- Server tells the client what to do: `429`/`503` + `Retry-After`; `409` for conflicts (don't retry blindly); `4xx` others are permanent.
- Clients: exponential backoff with jitter, capped attempts, retry budgets, no retry on non-idempotent calls without a key.
- Servers: deduplicate by key; make handlers safe to re-run; dead-letter after N failures.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="apid-retry-semantics">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="apid-pagination" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI API DESIGN</span><span class="rev-q">API design for AI and infrastructure services: pagination?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Opaque **cursor** (encodes position, stable under inserts) over offset/limit (skips/duplicates under change). Return `next_cursor`; cap page size; document ordering.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="apid-pagination">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="apid-rate-limits-quotas-admission-control" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI API DESIGN</span><span class="rev-q">API design for AI and infrastructure services: rate limits, quotas, admission control?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Rate limit per key/tenant/endpoint (token bucket), headers `X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset`. Quotas on scarce resources (GPU-seconds, storage bytes, concurrent jobs) with soft/hard tiers. Admission control inside: bounded queues per priority class, shed low-priority when saturated, estimate cost per request before admitting.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="apid-rate-limits-quotas-admission-control">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="apid-streaming-results" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI API DESIGN</span><span class="rev-q">API design for AI and infrastructure services: streaming results?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

For long generations or progressive outputs: server-sent events or chunked HTTP for one-way streams; WebSocket/gRPC streaming when bidirectional. Design for resumption (sequence numbers, `Last-Event-ID`), partial results on failure, and backpressure (client-driven flow control).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="apid-streaming-results">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="apid-versioning-and-compatibility" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI API DESIGN</span><span class="rev-q">API design for AI and infrastructure services: versioning and compatibility?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Version the API (path or header) and the **model** independently; let clients pin `model_version`; publish deprecation windows; never change the meaning of an existing field.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="apid-versioning-and-compatibility">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="apid-errors-that-help" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI API DESIGN</span><span class="rev-q">API design for AI and infrastructure services: errors that help?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Machine-readable code, human message, request id, retryable flag, and for jobs a `failure_reason` taxonomy (input invalid, quota exceeded, model error, infrastructure error).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="apid-errors-that-help">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="apid-interview-ready-statements" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI API DESIGN</span><span class="rev-q">API design for AI and infrastructure services: interview-ready statements?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- "Anything that touches a GPU is asynchronous behind a job API with idempotency keys."
- "Retries are a contract: the server says whether and when, the client obeys with jittered backoff and a budget."
- "Cursors, not offsets; quotas on the scarce resource, not just requests per second."

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="apid-interview-ready-statements">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Data and stores (17)

<p class="rev-plan">The store follows the access pattern. Say the pattern, then the store, then the nuance.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="store-transactions-money-status-machines-metadata-with" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">STORE</span><span class="rev-q">The requirement says transactions, money, status machines, metadata with joins. Which store, why, and the nuance?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Store.** Postgres, sharded by tenant or listing id past ~1 TB

**Why.** ACID, unique constraints as guards

**The nuance to say.** shard key is the one you look up by; read replicas for the read path; hot rows serialize at ~200/s

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="store-transactions-money-status-machines-metadata-with">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="store-counters-sessions-locks-rate-limits-anything-wit" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">STORE</span><span class="rev-q">The requirement says counters, sessions, locks, rate limits, anything with a TTL. Which store, why, and the nuance?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Store.** Redis cluster, shard by key

**Why.** sub-ms, atomic Lua, TTL cleans up

**The nuance to say.** not durable: never the booking truth, never the ledger; hot key for the biggest tenant, split it

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="store-counters-sessions-locks-rate-limits-anything-wit">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="store-high-write-rate-append-only-time-ordered-reads" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">STORE</span><span class="rev-q">The requirement says high write rate, append-only, time-ordered reads. Which store, why, and the nuance?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Store.** Cassandra / ScyllaDB, partition by (owner, time bucket)

**Why.** writes scale, one partition scan per read

**The nuance to say.** partitions under ~100 MB (add a bucket); no delete-on-ack queues (tombstones), use a flag + TTL; no joins

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="store-high-write-rate-append-only-time-ordered-reads">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="store-blobs-video-images-checkpoints-artifacts-archive" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">STORE</span><span class="rev-q">The requirement says blobs: video, images, checkpoints, artifacts, archives. Which store, why, and the nuance?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Store.** object storage, erasure coded

**Why.** cheapest durable bytes, presigned access

**The nuance to say.** lifecycle rules for expiry; listing is eventual; multipart for anything over a few MB

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="store-blobs-video-images-checkpoints-artifacts-archive">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="store-events-between-services-buffering-replay" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">STORE</span><span class="rev-q">The requirement says events between services, buffering, replay. Which store, why, and the nuance?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Store.** Kafka, partition by the key you aggregate on

**Why.** absorbs bursts, at-least-once, replay from offset

**The nuance to say.** order only inside a partition; retention bounds replay; consumer lag is the health signal; hot partition for a hot tenant

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="store-events-between-services-buffering-replay">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="store-full-text-or-vector-search" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">STORE</span><span class="rev-q">The requirement says full-text or vector search. Which store, why, and the nuance?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Store.** inverted index / ANN shards in RAM, document-partitioned, replicated

**Why.** every query to every shard, merge by raw score

**The nuance to say.** tail = slowest shard, hedge at p95; delta index for freshness; filters inside the shard

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="store-full-text-or-vector-search">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="store-time-series-metrics-dashboards" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">STORE</span><span class="rev-q">The requirement says time series, metrics, dashboards. Which store, why, and the nuance?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Store.** TSDB with roll-ups

**Why.** compression, cheap ranges

**The nuance to say.** cardinality is the limit: pre-aggregate per site or tenant

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="store-time-series-metrics-dashboards">got it</button></p>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-api-and-data-api-only-what-the-flows-need" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">API design & data modeling: aPI (only what the flows need)?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- Resource-oriented: `POST /jobs`, `GET /jobs/{id}`, `GET /jobs/{id}/results?cursor=`; verbs for actions that are not CRUD (`POST /jobs/{id}:cancel`).
- Every mutating call takes an **idempotency key**; every list call is **paginated with an opaque cursor**; every long operation returns **202 + job id**.
- Errors: 4xx = caller must change something, 5xx = retry with backoff, 429 = slow down (include `Retry-After`).
- Versioning: in the path or header; never break existing fields; add, deprecate, remove.
- Auth and tenancy on every request; quotas keyed by tenant.
- Payload discipline: bulk endpoints for hot paths; avoid chatty N+1 calls.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-api-and-data-api-only-what-the-flows-need">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-api-and-data-data-modeling" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">API design & data modeling: data modeling?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

1. Start from access patterns, not entities: "for each request, which key do I read/write?"
2. Choose the partition key from the hottest read; verify writes do not all land on one shard.
3. Decide what is a document (denormalised, read in one shot) vs what is a relation (needs joins/transactions).
4. Immutable/append-only where possible (events, versions) — simpler replication and audit.
5. Time-series: partition by time × entity; set retention/TTL up front.
6. Secondary indexes cost writes; every index is a second table to keep consistent.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-api-and-data-data-modeling">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-api-and-data-typical-entity-sketches" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">API design & data modeling: typical entity sketches?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- Object storage: `bucket/key → {version, size, checksum, chunks[], placement[], created}`; metadata store separate from bytes.
- Job system: `job {id, tenant, status, payload_ref, attempts, lease_owner, lease_expiry, idempotency_key, result_ref}`.
- Social/feed: `user`, `follow(user→user)`, `post`, `timeline(user, post_id, ts)` (fan-out on write vs read).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-api-and-data-typical-entity-sketches">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-storage-choi-storage-internals-worth-saying" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Database / storage choice: storage internals worth saying?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- LSM trees favour writes (sequential), pay on reads (levels, bloom filters) and compaction.
- B-trees favour reads and range scans; in-place writes.
- Write-ahead log + fsync is what durability means; group commit for throughput.
- Erasure coding (e.g. 8+4) ≈ 1.5× overhead vs 3× replication; costs CPU and cross-node reads on repair.
- Tiering: SSD hot / HDD warm / tape or cold object storage; promotion by access recency and frequency.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-storage-choi-storage-internals-worth-saying">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-storage-choi-media-delivery-vocabulary-from-day-1" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Database / storage choice: media delivery vocabulary (from Day 1)?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- **Codec** = how frames are compressed. **H.264/AVC**: universal, cheap to decode, larger files. **H.265/HEVC**: ~30-50 % smaller at the same quality, costlier to encode, patchier support. **AV1**: royalty-free, smaller still, slowest to encode. Transcoding = re-encoding one upload into several codec × resolution × bitrate renditions.
- **Container** = the file wrapping the encoded frames and audio (MP4, fMP4, MKV).
- **Adaptive bitrate streaming**: the video is cut into 2-10 s segments per rendition; the player switches renditions per segment based on measured bandwidth.
- **HLS** (Apple): playlist/manifest file **.m3u8** listing renditions and segment URLs (.ts or fMP4). **DASH** (MPEG): manifest **.mpd** (XML), fMP4 segments. Same idea, different manifest formats; players often support both.
- Interview line: "the transcoder writes renditions plus a manifest to object storage; the CDN serves manifest and segments; the player does the bitrate switching, so the origin never touches the hot path."

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-storage-choi-media-delivery-vocabulary-from-day-1">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="five-questions" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">FIVE QUESTIONS</span><span class="rev-q">The five questions that generate the nuances for any box?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

1. What is its unit of work, and what does one unit cost? (a request, a frame, a token, a chunk, a byte)
2. What state does it hold, and for how long? (none → disposable; seconds → ring buffer; a session → sticky with a map; forever → a store with a durability number)
3. What happens when it dies mid-work? (who notices, in how long, who takes over, what is replayed, what could be duplicated and what id prevents that)
4. What is its hot key? (the one tenant, celebrity, partition or row that gets all the traffic, and how it is split)
5. How does it find the others, and what happens when that lookup is stale? (session map, capacity view, config push, CDC; and the TTL or token that bounds the staleness)

**Remember by.** a story about any box: what it does and what one unit costs, what it holds, how it dies, who overloads it, how it finds the others.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="five-questions">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Caching: where a cache can live?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Client · CDN/edge · API gateway · application (in-process) · distributed cache (Redis/Memcached) · database buffer pool · storage tier (SSD in front of HDD).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-caching-where-a-cache-can-live">got it</button></p>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-caching-patterns" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Caching: patterns?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- **Cache-aside** (read-through by the app): simplest; stale until TTL or invalidation.
- **Write-through**: consistent, higher write latency. **Write-back**: fast writes, risk of loss.
- **Refresh-ahead** for predictable hot keys.
- **Negative caching** for "not found" storms.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-caching-patterns">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-caching-what-to-say-about-correctness" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Caching: what to say about correctness?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- Invalidation strategy: TTL, event-driven purge, versioned keys (`key@v7`).
- Stale reads: acceptable? For how long? Which flows must bypass the cache?
- Thundering herd: request coalescing / single-flight, jittered TTLs, stale-while-revalidate.
- Hot keys: replicate the key across nodes, local L1 cache, or shard by key + suffix.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-caching-what-to-say-about-correctness">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-caching-sizing-and-metrics" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Caching: sizing and metrics?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- Hit rate needed = 1 − backend_capacity/total_load. Track hit rate, p99 latency, evictions, memory fragmentation.
- Eviction: LRU default; LFU when a small set is very hot; TTL for freshness; size-aware for large objects.
- Consistent hashing with virtual nodes to add/remove cache nodes without mass misses.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-caching-sizing-and-metrics">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-caching-storage-tier-caching-ssd-in-front-of-hdd" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Caching: storage-tier caching (SSD in front of HDD)?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Admission policy (do not cache streaming scans), promotion on second hit, write-around for large sequential writes, read-ahead for known sequential access, per-tier hit-rate metrics.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-caching-storage-tier-caching-ssd-in-front-of-hdd">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-partitioning-partitioning-sharding" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Partitioning, replication, hotspots: partitioning (sharding)?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- **Hash** partitioning: even spread, no range scans. **Range**: scans and locality, risk of hot ranges (time!). **Directory**: lookup service maps key→shard, flexible, one more hop.
- Consistent hashing / virtual nodes for elastic membership; or fixed partition count with partition→node mapping (easier rebalancing).
- Rebalancing costs: data movement bandwidth, dual-writes during migration, client routing updates.
- Secondary indexes: local (scatter-gather reads) vs global (write to two shards).
- Choose the key so the hottest operation touches one shard; verify writes spread too.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-partitioning-partitioning-sharding">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-partitioning-replication" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Partitioning, replication, hotspots: replication?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- **Leader-based**: writes to leader, reads from followers (stale) or leader (fresh). Failover needs a new leader election and fencing of the old.
- **Multi-leader**: geo-writes, conflict resolution (LWW, CRDT, app-level).
- **Leaderless / quorum** (N, W, R with W+R>N): tunable consistency; read repair, hinted handoff.
- **Sync vs async** replication: durability vs write latency. Say the RPO/RTO consequence.
- Erasure coding for capacity tiers, replication for hot/low-latency tiers.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-partitioning-replication">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-consistency-what-each-costs" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Consistency: what each costs?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- Eventual consistency needs conflict handling: last-writer-wins (data loss risk), version vectors, CRDTs, or app-level merge.
- Session guarantees are often the sweet spot for user-facing features: route a user to the same replica, or carry a version token.

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-queues-strea-backpressure-the-part-senior-candidates-get-righ" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Queues, streams, backpressure: backpressure (the part senior candidates get right)?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- Bounded buffers everywhere; an unbounded queue just moves the failure to the OOM.
- Signals: queue depth, consumer lag, p99 latency, error rate. Actions: slow producers (429/credit-based flow control), shed load (drop lowest priority), degrade (cheaper path), scale consumers.
- Prefer **pull** by consumers at their own pace; producers observe lag.
- In pipelines (e.g. storage → decode → GPU): size each stage's buffer to cover the downstream's latency variance, no more; watch the slowest stage; batch to amortise per-item cost.

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-queues-strea-live-capture-ingest-webrtc-the-one-paragraph-ver" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Queues, streams, backpressure: live capture ingest (WebRTC) — the one-paragraph version?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

WebRTC is the browser/mobile standard for real-time media: the device negotiates a session through a **signalling** server (offer/answer, ICE candidates; STUN/TURN help it cross NATs), then streams encoded audio/video over UDP (SRTP) with congestion control, trading reliability for latency. In a capture pipeline the stream terminates at a media server (an **SFU** or ingest gateway) that either forwards it to viewers or, for storage, **records** it: the gateway re-packetises frames into segments (for example 2-8 s fragmented MP4), writes each segment to object storage as it closes, and publishes segment metadata as it goes. Consequences for design: many long-lived connections (state per stream, sticky routing to a gateway), the write path is a stream of small sequential segments per source rather than large uploads, "the object is complete" is an explicit end-of-stream event, and a gateway failure mid-stream must be resumable (client reconnects, segments already written are kept). Contrast with bulk ingest: large multipart uploads over HTTP, no session, no real-time constraint.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-queues-strea-live-capture-ingest-webrtc-the-one-paragraph-ver">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-coordination-coordination-primitives" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Distributed coordination & job scheduling: coordination primitives?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- **Consensus service** (ZooKeeper/etcd/Chubby): small, strongly consistent, for leader election, locks, membership, configuration. Not a data store.
- **Leader election**: ephemeral node/lease; new leader must **fence** the old one (epoch/fencing token carried on every write).
- **Distributed lock**: lease with TTL + heartbeat renewal; clients must handle lease expiry mid-work; prefer idempotent operations so a lost lock is not a disaster.
- **Membership & failure detection**: heartbeats, phi-accrual detectors, gossip for scale.
- **Clocks**: never trust wall clocks for ordering; use logical clocks, versions, or TrueTime-style bounded uncertainty.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-coordination-coordination-primitives">got it</button></p>

- Components: job store (definitions, schedules), scheduler (computes next run, enqueues), queue, workers with leases, result/status store, API.
- Guarantees to discuss: at-least-once with idempotent jobs; missed-run policy (skip, catch up, run once); exactly one scheduler active per partition (leader per shard).
- Scale: partition jobs by hash; time-wheel/priority heap per partition; avoid the thundering herd at :00 with jitter.
- Failure: worker dies mid-job → lease expires → redelivery; scheduler dies → new leader recomputes from persistent state; poison jobs → dead-letter + alert.
- Observability: scheduling delay, run duration histograms, failure rate, queue depth per priority.

## Deep-dive material: data paths, routing, AI infrastructure (26)

<p class="rev-plan">Where the bytes go, how a model is routed, and how GPUs change the design. This is what the two deep dives are made of.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-rule" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DATA PATH</span><span class="rev-q">Where do the bytes go? The rule to say.</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

"Queues carry references; bytes live where they are cheapest to keep for as long as they must wait: memory for a second, object storage for minutes or hours. The GPU never waits on a storage round trip for live work."

**Remember by.** bytes live where they are cheapest to keep for as long as they must wait: memory for a second, object storage for an hour.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-rule">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-sync" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DATA PATH</span><span class="rev-q">Sync call: where is the queue, where are the bytes, and which thread touches which counter?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Three kinds of threads, three kinds of state. A request handler is a lightweight task (goroutine, asyncio task), not an OS thread, so one gateway runs tens of thousands of them at once, one per open connection. Each handler owns its connection and its bytes; it is the only thing that touches the money counter in Redis, twice: an estimate at admission (arrow 2) and a settle with the worker's actual usage at the end (arrow 9), both as atomic Lua scripts because N gateways share the same bucket. The scheduler loop owns the local fairness state (deque lengths, deficit counters, in-flight per host) and never touches Redis. The config watcher receives the controller's weights and quota-divided-by-N every 5 seconds and swaps them in atomically, so the scheduler reads them without a lock. The bytes never enter the queue; the queue is a list of who waits.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-sync">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-stream" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DATA PATH</span><span class="rev-q">Stream: how do frames reach the GPU, and who decides the host?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

No queue system in the path: the stream gateway pushes each frame directly to the host that owns the session, and the only queue is a small in-memory buffer inside that host where frames wait for the next batch. The session router decides the host once, at open; the data plane never asks it again.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-stream">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-batch" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DATA PATH</span><span class="rev-q">Batch job: why object storage and Kafka?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Here the bytes are hours of video and may wait for hours, so they live in object storage and Kafka carries only chunk ids; a worker fetches a chunk's frames when its turn comes, and partial results go back to storage as each chunk finishes.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-batch">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-fair" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DATA PATH</span><span class="rev-q">Fair share across many gateways without a shared queue?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Why it adds up without a shared queue: the load balancer gives every gateway the same mix of tenants, so N local 5/3/1 schedulers behave like one global 5/3/1; the controller gives every gateway the same weights and each tenant's quota divided by N, and moves shares between gateways when the reported usage is skewed. The one case that breaks the picture is a tenant stuck on few gateways (a sticky hash); that tenant is handled by a shared Redis bucket or a central admission service instead.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-fair">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-controller" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DATA PATH</span><span class="rev-q">What the controller does, in one line?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

gateways report usage every 5 seconds, the controller sums it, splits each quota across gateways in proportion, and pushes the same versioned config to all of them

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-controller">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-counters" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DATA PATH</span><span class="rev-q">Who updates which counter? The sentence to say.</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Redis holds the money counter, updated by the request handler with an estimate-then-settle pair of atomic scripts. The scheduler holds only local fairness state. The controller refreshes the shares every 5 seconds and the config watcher swaps them in.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-counters">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-router" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DATA PATH</span><span class="rev-q">Inside the model gateway: router and serving process, what to say?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

the router is a lookup, the bytes make one gRPC hop from the gateway to the host's serving process, the host batches whatever is waiting into each GPU step, and streams tokens back on the same connection; capacity flows the other way once a second so the router never sends to a full host.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-router">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-push" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DATA PATH</span><span class="rev-q">Does the scheduler push to the GPU host, or does the worker pull? And if asked why not pull?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Push. The scheduler makes a gRPC call on a pooled, long-lived connection to the serving process on host H and sends the bytes inside the call. The worker never pulls. Pull needs the worker to know which gateway holds work, which means a broker in the middle, and that is the hop you avoid for a sub-second call. Backpressure comes from the host instead: it keeps a bounded queue, rejects fast with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED when full, and the scheduler retries on another host. That retry is rare because the router's 1-second capacity view already steered the request away from full hosts. Pull is the right shape in diagram 3, where workers pull chunk ids from Kafka because the wait is long and the bytes sit in object storage.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-push">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="dp-settle" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">DATA PATH</span><span class="rev-q">Why charge an estimate at admission and settle at completion?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Why the estimate and the settle: it is the card authorization pattern. The gateway must decide admission before the work runs, and nobody knows the output token count until generation ends, so it reserves the worst case (input estimate plus max_output_tokens) and settles to the actual number at the end. Charging nothing until the end would let a tenant launch 1,000 concurrent requests and pass its quota before the first one finished. A reservation carries a TTL of a minute or two, so a gateway crash cannot leave tokens reserved forever, and a reaper reconciles from the Kafka usage events. A tenant that sets a huge max_output_tokens reserves more per call and gets fewer concurrent calls, which is the right incentive.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="dp-settle">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="route-dims" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">MODEL ROUTING</span><span class="rev-q">What do you route on? Name the dimensions before the mechanism.</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

| Dimension | Signal | Example decision |
|---|---|---|
| Difficulty and quality | prompt length, task type, a small classifier, the user's tier | easy classification to the 8B model, open reasoning to the large model |
| Cost and budget | tenant plan, remaining daily budget, tokens in the request | budget nearly spent: downgrade to the cheaper model, never refuse silently |
| Latency budget | the caller's deadline, interactive against batch | interactive under 1 s to the small model or a warm large replica; batch to the cheapest queue |
| Modality and features | image, video, audio, tools, context length | 2-hour video to the long-context model; a frame to the vision model |
| Version and experiment | model alias, canary percentage, A/B bucket by key | 5% of keys to v2, sticky per key so a conversation never flips versions |
| Capacity and locality | replica queue depth, KV-cache or prefix-cache hit, GPU pool health | route the next turn to the replica that already holds this conversation's cache |
| Region and data rules | tenant residency, on-premises requirement | EU tenant never leaves EU pools |
| Fallback | provider error rate, rate-limit responses, timeouts | after two 429s from the vendor, fail over to own pool for 60 s |

Say the dimension first ("this is capacity-aware routing") and the interviewer knows you know the taxonomy.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="route-dims">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="route-say" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">MODEL ROUTING</span><span class="rev-q">Model routing in 60 seconds, said in the interview?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

"Requests come through the gateway with tenant, tier, modality and size. A stateless router reads a policy from the registry and a one-second capacity view from the replicas, and picks a pool. Rules and heuristics do most of the routing; a small classifier separates easy from hard prompts once we have judged logs; the batch path uses a cascade because latency is cheap there. Conversations and streams are routed once and stay on their replica for cache and state locality, with a session map for failover. New versions enter behind the same alias at a small percentage per tenant, judged on quality as well as latency, rolled back by a policy change. Every decision is logged with a reason so cost and quality can be explained per tenant."

See also: board 2, deep dive B (aliases, canary per key, rollback by pointer flip).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="route-say">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="route-pushes" data-kind="say">

<details class="rev" data-card="aiinf-training-vs-inference" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI INFRASTRUCTURE</span><span class="rev-q">AI infrastructure: training vs inference?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

| | Training | Inference |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | Long-running job, many GPUs in lockstep, epochs over a dataset | Request-driven, many small independent calls |
| Bottleneck | Data feed + interconnect + checkpoint I/O | Latency per request, GPU memory, batching |
| Failure cost | Lost work since last checkpoint × all GPUs | One failed request; retry |
| Storage pattern | Massive sequential/random reads of the dataset; periodic huge writes (checkpoints) | Model weights read at load time; results written per request |

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="aiinf-training-vs-inference">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="aiinf-online-vs-batch-inference" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI INFRASTRUCTURE</span><span class="rev-q">AI infrastructure: online vs batch inference?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Online: latency SLO (tens to hundreds of ms), request queue, small dynamic batches, warm models resident on GPUs. Batch: throughput SLO, large static batches, can run on cheaper/preemptible capacity, results to storage.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="aiinf-online-vs-batch-inference">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="aiinf-batching-and-dynamic-batching" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI INFRASTRUCTURE</span><span class="rev-q">AI infrastructure: batching and dynamic batching?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Batching amortises weight reads and kernel launches: throughput rises roughly linearly with batch size until compute saturates; latency rises too. **Dynamic batching** waits up to a small window (e.g. 5-20 ms) to collect requests, then runs one batch; tune window vs p99. For LLMs, *continuous batching* admits new sequences as others finish.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="aiinf-batching-and-dynamic-batching">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="aiinf-gpu-utilisation-and-memory" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI INFRASTRUCTURE</span><span class="rev-q">AI infrastructure: gPU utilisation and memory?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- Utilisation = fraction of time kernels run. Idle causes: waiting for data, CPU preprocessing, small batches, synchronisation stalls, host↔device copies.
- Memory = weights + activations (∝ batch × sequence) + optimizer state (training, 2-3× weights) + KV cache (inference). Out of memory → smaller batch, mixed precision, sharding weights, offloading.
- Rule of thumb: fp16 weights = 2 bytes/param; 7B ≈ 14 GB, 70B ≈ 140 GB.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="aiinf-gpu-utilisation-and-memory">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="aiinf-cpu-preprocessing-prefetch-data-loaders" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI INFRASTRUCTURE</span><span class="rev-q">AI infrastructure: cPU preprocessing, prefetch, data loaders?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

The data loader decodes (video/JPEG), augments, shuffles, batches, and pins memory before the GPU step. Use many CPU workers per GPU, **prefetch** N batches ahead into a bounded buffer, overlap host→device copies with compute. Measure *data wait time* per step; if it is non-zero the GPU is starving. For video: decoding is expensive — consider pre-decoded/pre-chunked formats, GPU decoding, or a preprocessing tier.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="aiinf-cpu-preprocessing-prefetch-data-loaders">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="aiinf-model-placement-and-versioning" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI INFRASTRUCTURE</span><span class="rev-q">AI infrastructure: model placement and versioning?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Placement: which GPUs hold which model (memory fit, load time, traffic). Warm pools and lazy loading trade cost for cold-start latency. **Versioning**: immutable model artifacts with content hashes; a registry maps `model:version → artifact`; requests may pin a version; rollouts are canaried; rollback = flip the pointer.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="aiinf-model-placement-and-versioning">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="aiinf-checkpointing" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI INFRASTRUCTURE</span><span class="rev-q">AI infrastructure: checkpointing?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Periodic snapshot of weights + optimizer state to durable storage. Cadence balances lost-work-on-failure vs write cost (a checkpoint can be hundreds of GB and stall training if synchronous). Techniques: asynchronous checkpointing from a CPU copy, sharded checkpoints written in parallel, keep last N, verify by checksum, resume from checkpoint on failure.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="aiinf-checkpointing">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="aiinf-data-parallelism-vs-model-parallelism" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI INFRASTRUCTURE</span><span class="rev-q">AI infrastructure: data parallelism vs model parallelism?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- **Data parallel**: every GPU has the full model, processes a different shard of the batch, gradients are all-reduced each step. Interconnect bandwidth matters; the slowest GPU sets the pace.
- **Model parallel**: the model is split across GPUs — tensor parallel (split layers), pipeline parallel (split stages; needs micro-batches to avoid bubbles). Used when the model does not fit.
- Real systems combine them (3D parallelism) and shard optimizer state (ZeRO/FSDP).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="aiinf-data-parallelism-vs-model-parallelism">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="aiinf-stragglers" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI INFRASTRUCTURE</span><span class="rev-q">AI infrastructure: stragglers?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

In synchronous training one slow worker delays every step. Causes: bad hardware, thermal throttling, noisy neighbour, slow storage path. Mitigations: detect via per-step timing, replace the node, speculative/backup work for input fetching, asynchronous or bounded-staleness variants for some workloads.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="aiinf-stragglers">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="aiinf-backpressure-in-ai-pipelines" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI INFRASTRUCTURE</span><span class="rev-q">AI infrastructure: backpressure in AI pipelines?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Bounded queues between storage → decode → GPU; when GPU is the bottleneck the loader should idle rather than fill RAM; when storage is the bottleneck, increase parallelism/prefetch or fix locality. Expose queue depths per stage.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="aiinf-backpressure-in-ai-pipelines">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="aiinf-interview-ready-statements" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">AI INFRASTRUCTURE</span><span class="rev-q">AI infrastructure: interview-ready statements?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- "GPU time is the currency; I design the storage and CPU tiers so the accelerator never waits."
- "Checkpoint cadence is the RPO of a training job."
- "Dynamic batching trades p99 latency for throughput; the window is a tunable I would expose per model."

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="aiinf-interview-ready-statements">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="aigpu-essentials" data-kind="say">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">GPU INFRASTRUCTURE</span><span class="rev-q">AI and GPU infrastructure: the design-interview essentials?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

Deeper treatment in AI infrastructure. The design-interview essentials:
- **GPUs are the cost centre.** Every design question becomes "how do I keep utilisation high?": batching, prefetch, fast storage, avoiding CPU bottlenecks, avoiding stragglers.
- **Training**: long-running, synchronous across many GPUs (data parallel), needs checkpoints (large, periodic, to durable storage), a data pipeline that never starves the accelerators, and restart-from-checkpoint on failure.
- **Inference**: request-driven; online (latency-bound, dynamic batching windows of a few ms) vs batch (throughput-bound). Model loading time drives placement and warm pools. Model versions must be pinnable and rollback-able.
- **Data pipeline**: storage → (network) → CPU decode/preprocess → host RAM buffer → GPU. Size buffers to cover latency variance; measure "GPU waiting for data" directly.
- **Memory**: model weights + activations + KV cache must fit; batch size trades throughput for memory; sharding weights across GPUs (tensor/pipeline parallel) when they do not fit.
- **Failures**: a straggler slows every synchronous step; detect and replace; checkpoint cadence = acceptable lost work.
- **Numbers**: a training job may read 1-5 GB/s per node; a 70B-parameter model ≈ 140 GB in fp16; H100 ≈ 3 TB/s HBM, 80 GB.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="aigpu-essentials">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-failure-reco-standard-mitigations" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Failure handling & recovery: standard mitigations?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- **Timeouts** on every call; **retries** with exponential backoff + jitter and a retry budget; **idempotency keys** so retries are safe.
- **Circuit breakers** and **bulkheads** (isolate pools per dependency).
- **Health checks** distinct from readiness; remove from rotation before killing.
- **Replication** for availability, **erasure coding** for durability at lower cost, **checksums** end to end to detect corruption, **scrubbing** to find it early.
- **Leases + fencing** so exactly one worker acts; **heartbeats** to detect the dead.
- **Graceful degradation**: read-only mode, stale cache, reduced features.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-failure-reco-standard-mitigations">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="pp-failure-reco-recovery" data-kind="read">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">PATTERN PAGE</span><span class="rev-q">Failure handling & recovery: recovery?</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

- RPO (data you may lose) and RTO (time to be back) drive backup cadence, replication mode, failover automation.
- Rebuild after disk/node loss: repair bandwidth budget vs foreground traffic, prioritise the most-degraded data (fewest surviving replicas/fragments first).
- Replay from log/checkpoint; snapshots + WAL; point-in-time recovery.
- Runbooks and game days; automate the common failures, page for the rare ones.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="pp-failure-reco-recovery">got it</button></p>

</div>
</details>

Alert on symptoms (SLO burn rate) not causes; page only for user-visible impact; every alert has a runbook; watch for alert fatigue.

<div class="rev-a">
